overview: The MORE WATER Act changes several Western water programs run by the Interior Department's Bureau of Reclamation. It extends a grant program for large water recycling projects from five to ten years, lets it fund feasibility studies, and raises the federal funding ceiling for individual water recycling projects under an older program from $20 million to $50 million, adjusted each year for inflation. It extends certain provisions of a 2016 water law, the Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation (WIIN) Act, including authority for actions to help endangered species from 2028 through 2032, such as habitat work at Utah's Great Salt Lake (only at the state's request) and salmon and steelhead restoration, monitoring, and hatchery upgrades on California's Sacramento River. It also sets up a process to cancel the approval of Reclamation projects that have received no federal funding for about eight years, with the department publishing lists and projects deauthorized two years later unless Congress funds them, Congress disapproves, a local sponsor pays to finish them, or the department deems them vital. As of September 17, 2026, a Senate committee had approved it with changes and it was placed on the Senate calendar for possible floor action.
for: Supporters say the bill gives drought-prone communities more tools for recycled water and fish recovery, while clearing out a backlog of stalled, unfunded projects so active ones can move forward.
against: Critics say raising funding ceilings and extending programs expands federal spending commitments, and automatic deauthorization could end projects that some communities still want simply because funding has been slow.
